# block B — fitting and specifying [01:00 – 01:39]{.tm} {#block-b}

## B1 · the dyad-independent model, and a confusing thing the console says [01:00 – 01:13]{.tm}

let us fit something. start with the two questions we can answer without any dependence at
all: grade homophily and sex homophily. i will add `nodecov("Grade")` too, which asks whether
older students simply have more friends.

```{r}
#| label: b1-fit
m1 <- fit_or_load("m1_dyadindep",
  ergm(mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Sex") +
         nodecov("Grade"),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

```{r}
#| label: b1-summary
summary(m1)
```

under a second. no MCMC, no diagnostics needed, no chance of degeneracy. why?

```{r}
#| label: b1-dyadindep
is.dyad.independent(m1)
```

every term in that model has a change statistic that depends only on nodes $i$ and $j$. so the
dyads *are* conditionally independent, the model factors into a product over dyads, and the
whole thing is exactly a logistic regression on the $\binom{205}{2} = 20{,}910$ dyads.

### the thing that confuses everyone

watch the console when that fits. it says **"Starting maximum pseudolikelihood estimation
(MPLE)... Finished MPLE."** but ask the object what it did:

```{r}
#| label: b1-estimate
m1$estimate
```

it says **MLE**. so which is it?

both, and they are the same thing here. the pseudolikelihood is the product of the conditional
probabilities of each dyad given the rest. when the model is dyad-independent, those
conditionals *are* independent, so the pseudolikelihood **is** the likelihood — not an
approximation to it, literally it. `ergm` runs the MPLE machinery because it is fast, and then
correctly labels the result MLE because that is what it is.

when the model is dyad-dependent, that equivalence breaks and MPLE becomes a genuine
approximation with genuinely understated standard errors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — which estimator, and when: the three-line rule"}
this is the decision rule i would actually give you, and it has changed since the 2008 JSS
paper you were assigned:

**dyad-independent model** → it is exact logistic regression. instant, no MCMC, no diagnostics.
nothing can go wrong.

**dyad-dependent, up to roughly a couple of thousand nodes** → MCMC-MLE, which is the default.
let `ergm` choose its own sample size.

**bigger than that** → MPLE, *but* you must change how the standard errors are computed.
Schmid & Desmarais (2017) show MPLE point estimates are fine while the naive standard errors
are badly understated; their parametric bootstrap gives correct coverage at about a fifth of
the cost of MCMLE. this is now built in — but **it is not the default**:

```{r}
#| label: b1-mplecov
eval(formals(control.ergm)$MPLE.covariance.method)
```

`invHess` is the one that understates. if you are using MPLE on a dependent model, set
`MPLE.covariance.method = "bootstrap"` (or `"Godambe"`) and say in your paper that you did.

**contrastive divergence** (`estimate = "CD"`) exists, and Krivitsky (2017) introduced it
precisely as a way to seed MCMLE. the literature here is genuinely mixed and the honest answer
is: MPLE is the current default seed and works well, so reach for CD only when you have a
specific reason (some hard-to-initialise curved models), and check convergence carefully if you
do. ask me if you have a case.
:::

```{r}
#| label: offroad-1
#| eval: false
# ---- live space: questions from the room go here ----
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-checkpoint
checkpoint(coefs = round(coef(m1), 3), label = "CHECKPOINT B1")
```

## B2 · what the numbers mean, in units a human can use [01:13 – 01:23]{.tm} {#b2}

we have `nodematch.Grade` $\approx$ `r round(coef(m1)[["nodematch.Grade"]], 2)`. what is that,
in units anybody outside this room would accept?

### step one: the baseline

start with the simplest possible reading. a model with only `edges` has a constant change
statistic of 1 for every dyad, so the log-odds of any tie is just that one coefficient, and:

```{r}
#| label: b2-baseline
m0 <- fit_or_load("m0_edges",
  ergm(mesa ~ edges, control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
c(coef_edges = coef(m0)[["edges"]],
  implied_prob = plogis(coef(m0)[["edges"]]),
  observed_density = network.density(mesa))
```

`plogis()` of the `edges` coefficient recovers the density exactly. `plogis()` is the
inverse-logit — the $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}$ that appears in the formulas above. that is a useful
sanity check and it makes concrete that `edges` is the intercept.

### step two: why you cannot just exponentiate and stop

the tempting move is $e^{2.95} \approx 19$ — "same-grade pairs have 19 times the odds." that
is arithmetically true and it is a conditional odds ratio, so it is *defensible*. but odds
ratios on a network this sparse are close to useless for conveying magnitude to a reader, and
there is a second problem that is worse.

::: {.callout-warning title="the rule that matters most for reading other people's papers"}
**do not compare ERGM coefficients across nested specifications.**

this is Duxbury (2023, *Sociological Methods & Research*). an ERGM is a logistic-form model
with a fixed residual variance, so — exactly as in ordinary logit — adding a term rescales
*all* the other coefficients, **even terms that are uncorrelated with it**. so when a paper
shows you model 1, model 2, model 3 and says "the homophily effect shrinks once we control for
triadic closure," that sentence is not supported by the numbers shown. the change in the
coefficient confounds a real change with a pure rescaling.

you will see this in print constantly. here is how you catch a broken ERGM paper — and in this
literature you will, constantly: it is one of the six questions on the referee checklist at the
end of today.
:::

### step three: average marginal effects

the fix is to put everything on the probability scale, where rescaling is not an issue and
where the number means something. this is the single most useful eight minutes of the day for
communicating your results to people who do not do this.

the average marginal effect of term $k$ is

$$\mathrm{AME}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{ij \in \mathcal{D}} p_{ij}(1 - p_{ij}) \cdot \theta_k , \qquad p_{ij} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\theta^{\top}\delta(y_{ij})\right)$$

which is the ordinary logit AME, computed dyad by dyad using the change statistics from
[A3](#a3). it is three lines of code rather than a black box — read them once now, line by
line tonight:

```{r}
#| label: b2-amefun
ame <- function(fit, term) {
  mp <- ergmMPLE(fit$formula, output = "dyadlist",
                 basis = fit$network)
  th <- coef(fit)
  X  <- mp$predictor[, names(th), drop = FALSE]  # delta, all dyads
  p  <- plogis(as.vector(X %*% th))              # fitted tie prob
  s  <- mean(p * (1 - p))                        # logistic scale
  c(AME = s * th[[term]], scale = s)
}
```

`ergmMPLE(..., output = "dyadlist")` hands you the change statistic matrix for every dyad —
the same $\delta(y_{ij})$ we computed by hand in [A3](#a3), just for all 20,910 of them at
once. that is the only non-obvious line.

now watch what happens when we apply it to a **dense** network and a **sparse** one. first the
monastery — 18 monks, sampson's classic data, and dense enough that a probability change is
legible:

```{r}
#| label: b2-sampson
data(sampson)
s1 <- fit_or_load("s1_sampson",
  ergm(samplike ~ edges + nodematch("group") + mutual,
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
data.frame(estimate = round(coef(s1), 3))
ame(s1, "nodematch.group")
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

**on average, two monks being in the same faction raises the probability of a nomination by
about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*ame(s1, "nodematch.group")[["AME"]])`
percentage points.** that sentence you can put in an abstract. "2.32" you cannot.

now the same computation on mesa:

```{r}
#| label: b2-mesa-ame
ame(m1, "nodematch.Grade")
c(density = network.density(mesa))
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-compare
#| echo: false
a_s <- ame(s1, "nodematch.group")
a_m <- ame(m1, "nodematch.Grade")
```

here is a puzzle, and i want you to feel it before i resolve it. mesa's same-grade coefficient
is *larger* than sampson's — `r round(coef(m1)[["nodematch.Grade"]],2)` vs
`r round(coef(s1)[["nodematch.group"]],2)` — so which network has the bigger effect on the
probability scale?

the answer is sampson, and it is not close: **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100*a_m[["AME"]])` percentage
points** on mesa against sampson's `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*a_s[["AME"]])`, an AME about
**`r sprintf("%.0f", a_s[["AME"]]/a_m[["AME"]])` times smaller** despite the *larger*
coefficient. that is not a contradiction and it is not a bug — it is the most important
practical lesson about marginal effects on networks.

look at the `scale` term the function returned, $\overline{p(1-p)}$: it is
`r sprintf("%.3f", a_s[["scale"]])` on sampson and only
`r sprintf("%.4f", a_m[["scale"]])` on mesa — a factor of about
`r sprintf("%.0f", a_s[["scale"]]/a_m[["scale"]])`. in a network with density under one
percent, essentially every dyad sits far out in the flat tail of the logistic curve, where
even a large shift in log-odds moves the probability barely at all. a nineteen-fold change in
odds against a baseline of `r round(network.density(mesa),4)` is still a small absolute
probability.

::: {.callout-important title="so report both, always"}
on a sparse network an AME reported alone will make a real, large effect look trivial, and a
coefficient reported alone will make it look enormous. **report the AME next to the baseline
density.** "same-grade pairs are `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*a_m[["AME"]])` percentage points more
likely to be friends, against a baseline density of
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100*network.density(mesa))` percent" is honest and complete. together those
two numbers tell you the shift is about
**`r sprintf("%.1f", a_m[["AME"]]/network.density(mesa))`× the baseline density itself** —
substantively large — while still being small on an absolute scale. either half on its own is
misleading.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — two caveats on that AME, and the packaged version"}
**first**, the change statistics come from `ergmMPLE` evaluated at the **observed** network.
for a dyad-independent model that is exactly right. for a dependent model it is a
*conditional-on-the-observed-graph* marginal effect, not a marginal effect under the model's
own equilibrium distribution. it is the standard thing everybody reports, and it is what the
package below reports too, but it is worth knowing what it conditions on.

**second**, the formula above is the *derivative* marginal effect. for a binary term you could
instead take the discrete difference, $\overline{\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta + \theta_k) -
\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta)}$, where $\eta$ is the linear predictor with that term switched off.

```{r}
#| label: b2-discrete
#| echo: false
.mp  <- ergmMPLE(s1$formula, output = "dyadlist", basis = s1$network)
.th  <- coef(s1); .k <- "nodematch.group"
.X   <- .mp$predictor[, names(.th), drop = FALSE]
.eta0 <- as.vector(.X %*% .th) - .X[, .k] * .th[[.k]]
dd_s <- mean(plogis(.eta0 + .th[[.k]]) - plogis(.eta0))
```

these agree when effects are small and diverge when they are not: on sampson the derivative
version gives `r sprintf("%.3f", ame(s1, "nodematch.group")[["AME"]])` and the discrete version
gives about `r sprintf("%.2f", dd_s)`. neither is wrong; say which you used.

**the packaged version** is `ergMargins::ergm.AME()` (Duxbury), which computes exactly the
derivative formula above plus a delta-method standard error. i have checked our three lines
against it and they agree to five decimal places. i am teaching the arithmetic rather than the
package for two reasons: you can see what it does, and it is one less thing to install for 37
people. if you want the standard errors and the mediation/moderation tools,
`install.packages("ergMargins")` — it is on CRAN, and `vif.ergm()` in the same package is a
cheap way to diagnose the near-collinearity that produces "linear dependence detected among
model statistics" warnings.
:::

### tiered exercise (take-home — we will not work it live)

> in the room i will read the core prompt and flash the solution tab; the working-through is
> yours, tonight. everything is instant and seeded, so your numbers will match mine exactly.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## core

compute the change statistic for the `nodecov("Grade")` term, by hand, for the pair (1, 2),
and confirm it against `summary()`. fill in the blank:

```{r}
#| label: b2-ex-core
#| eval: false
delta_ij(mesa, 1, 2, ~ ______)
```

then say in one sentence what `nodecov("Grade")` tests that `nodematch("Grade")` does not.

## stretch

the `nodecov("Grade")` coefficient is small (`r round(coef(m1)[["nodecov.Grade"]], 3)`) but
strongly significant. compute its AME. then explain why an AME is a slightly odd thing to
report for this particular term, and what you would report instead.

## solution

```{r}
#| label: b2-ex-soln
delta_ij(mesa, 1, 2, ~ nodecov("Grade"))
```

**core.** `nodecov("Grade")` sums the grade values of the two endpoints, so its change
statistic is $\text{grade}_i + \text{grade}_j$ = `r grade[1]` + `r grade[2]` =
`r grade[1] + grade[2]`. `nodematch` asks whether *similarity* drives ties — do 9th graders
befriend 9th graders. `nodecov` asks whether the *level* drives ties — do older students have
more friends regardless of who those friends are. one is homophily, the other is activity, and
a network can easily have one without the other.

**stretch.**

```{r}
#| label: b2-ex-soln2
ame(m1, "nodecov.Grade")
```

the AME is tiny, but the deeper problem is that `nodecov("Grade")` is not binary — its change
statistic ranges from `r 2*min(grade)` to `r 2*max(grade)`. so "the average marginal effect"
is the effect of a **one-unit increase in the summed grades of the pair**, which is not a
quantity anyone has an intuition about. better to report the effect of moving one endpoint up
a full grade (multiply by 1, since one endpoint moving up one grade raises the sum by one), or
better still, report predicted tie probabilities at a few substantively chosen grade
combinations. this is the general lesson: AMEs are cleanest for binary terms and need thought
for continuous ones.
:::

```{r}
#| label: b2-checkpoint
checkpoint(ame_sampson = ame(s1, "nodematch.group")[["AME"]],
           ame_mesa    = ame(m1, "nodematch.Grade")[["AME"]],
           label = "CHECKPOINT B2")
```

## B3 · endogenous terms — the reason you are here [01:23 – 01:39]{.tm}

everything so far you could have done with a logistic regression and the right standard
errors. now we do the thing that only an ERGM does: put a **structural** feature of the
network into the model as a parameter.

### reciprocity

the first and simplest endogenous term is `mutual`: if $i$ names $j$, is $j$ more likely to
name $i$?

and here we hit a genuine constraint that is worth stating out loud, because it teaches
something about how these terms work:

```{r}
#| label: b3-directed
is.directed(mesa)
```

mesa is **undirected**. a friendship there is a single symmetric object — there is no such
thing as $i \to j$ without $j \to i$, so reciprocity is not a question you can ask. try it and
`ergm` will refuse. this is not an inconvenience; it is the model telling you that term
availability is a property of *your data*, not a menu you choose from.

so reciprocity goes on sampson, which is directed — 18 monks each nominating the others.

```{r}
#| label: b3-mutual
round(summary(s1)$coefficients, 3)
```

`mutual` = `r round(coef(s1)[["mutual"]], 2)`, and its change statistic is 1 exactly when the
reciprocal tie $ji$ is already present, 0 otherwise. so: conditional on everything else,
a nomination that would *reciprocate* an existing one has `r round(coef(s1)[["mutual"]], 2)`
more log-odds than one that would not. on the probability scale:

```{r}
#| label: b3-mutual-ame
ame(s1, "mutual")
```

about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*ame(s1, "mutual")[["AME"]])` percentage
points. reciprocity is a big deal in this monastery, which if you have read sampson is not a
surprise.

### the term vocabulary is searchable — do not memorize it

`edges`, `nodematch`, `nodecov`, `mutual` — where do these names come from? a term database
that ships inside `ergm` itself, several hundred entries deep across the statnet packages.
nobody holds that in their head, and you should not try, because the package has a built-in
search engine and using it is the single habit that separates people who fight this software
from people who use it.

```{r}
#| label: b3-search
search.ergmTerms(search = "geometrically weighted edgewise")
search.ergmTerms(name = "nonzero")
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

two lookups, two lessons. `search =` scans the *descriptions* and finds `gwesp` — hold that
name, it is the repair for the disaster we are going to cause on purpose after the break. and
read its signature closely: `fixed=FALSE` is the default, which is a loaded gun we come back
to in [C1](#c1). `name =` wants an exact term name, and the second call misses — but the miss
tells you the fix. (`nonzero` is real; it lives in the *valued* vocabulary, and it is the
hinge of [C3](#c3).)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="three more searches to run on your own time — off the clock"}
* `search.ergmTerms(keywords = "triad-related")` — all 17 closure-adjacent terms in one screen.
* `search.ergmTerms(keywords = "curved")` — the geometrically weighted family; every single
  signature defaults to `fixed = FALSE`.
* `search.ergmConstraints("degree")` and `search.ergmReferences("discrete")` — the same engine
  for the `constraints =` and `reference =` arguments, the other two vocabularies you will
  eventually need (the second one matters this afternoon, in [C3](#c3)).
:::

### transitivity, and the naive way to ask for it

back to mesa, and to question 3 from [A1](#a1): are friendships transitive?

the obvious term is `triangle`, which literally counts triangles. we already know there are
`r summary(mesa ~ triangle)` of them. so the specification writes itself:

```{r}
#| label: b3-naive
#| eval: false
ergm(mesa ~ edges + triangle)
```

that is the natural thing to write, it is what the term is called, and it is what a reasonable
person would try first.

do not run it yet. we are running it together after the break, and i want you watching the
console when we do.

```{r}
#| label: b3-checkpoint
checkpoint(mutual_coef = coef(s1)[["mutual"]],
           mesa_triangles = summary(mesa ~ triangle),
           label = "CHECKPOINT B3")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="the full toolbox — specification terms we did not need today · self-study, not on the clock"}
the timed path uses the smallest set of terms that carries the ideas. these are the ones you
will reach for first in real work. every chunk runs as-is; none is required for anything else
today.

**descriptives before you fit.** `degreedist()` is the ten-second look at the degree
distribution, and `isolates` + `degree(d)` are the model-term versions of the same facts:

```{r}
#| label: tb-spec-desc
degreedist(mesa)
summary(mesa ~ isolates + degree(0:3))
```

`r summary(mesa ~ isolates)[[1]]` of `r network.size(mesa)` students are isolates. that is not a nuisance — it is
a quarter of your nodes, and a model whose simulated networks have no isolates is wrong in a
way `gof()`'s degree panel will catch ([C2](#c2)).

**homophily beyond `nodematch`.** if your attribute is genuinely continuous, a referee will
expect `absdiff` — the sum of $|x_i - x_j|$ over edges, so a *negative* coefficient means
similarity attracts. and `nodemix` is the model-term version of the `mixingmatrix()` we use in
[C2](#c2): one parameter per attribute-pair cell instead of one per diagonal.

```{r}
#| label: tb-spec-homoph
summary(mesa ~ absdiff("Grade"))
summary(mesa ~ nodemix("Grade", levels2 = -1))
```

note the empty off-diagonal cells (`mix.Grade.7.8` = 0, `mix.Grade.7.9` = 0): fit `nodemix`
here naively and you buy the same `-Inf` problem [C2](#c2) demonstrates for `Race` — same
disease, same `mixingmatrix()`-first cure. (`levels2 = -1` drops the first cell as the
reference; that default flipped in ergm 4 — see [appendix A](#appendix-a).)

**degree-based dependence.** `gwdegree` is to *popularity* what `gwesp` is to *closure* — a
geometrically weighted count that damps the runaway feedback — and it carries exactly the same
silent `fixed = TRUE` trap from [C1](#c1). directed versions: `gwidegree` / `gwodegree`.

```{r}
#| label: tb-spec-gwdeg
summary(mesa ~ gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE))
```

**dyadic covariates — the one this box exists for.** half of this room is IR, and every
gravity-style question — does trade follow alliances? do wave-1 ties predict wave-3 ties? —
is a *dyadic covariate* question. `edgecov(x)` puts an entire matrix on the right-hand side:
its change statistic for dyad $ij$ is simply $x_{ij}$. sampson's three waves make a clean
demonstration — predict wave 3 from wave 1:

```{r}
#| label: tb-spec-edgecov
data(samplk)
ec <- fit_or_load("tb_edgecov",
  ergm(samplk3 ~ edges + mutual + edgecov(as.matrix(samplk1)),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
round(summary(ec)$coefficients, 3)
```

a wave-1 nomination raises the log-odds of the same wave-3 nomination by
`r round(coef(ec)[["edgecov.as.matrix(samplk1)"]], 2)`, over and above reciprocity. that is a
hand-rolled lagged-network term — and a two-line preview of [C4](#c4), where the lag stops
being hand-rolled and becomes the model. the sibling `dyadcov(x)` fits separate parameters by
dyad type for directed data.

**term operators — the vocabulary became compositional in ergm 4.** appendix A lists them
(`B()`, `F()`, `Offset()`, `Symmetrize()`, ...); here is one actually running. `F(formula,
filter)` evaluates a statistic on the *subgraph of dyads that satisfy the filter*:

```{r}
#| label: tb-spec-operator
summary(samplike ~ F(~edges, ~nodematch("group")) + nodematch("group"))
f_op <- ergm(samplike ~ edges + F(~edges, ~nodematch("group")),
             control = snctrl(seed = 6886))
round(coef(f_op), 3)
```

both statistics are `r summary(samplike ~ nodematch("group"))[[1]]` — "edges, restricted to
within-group dyads" *is* the `nodematch` count, rebuilt from parts. so the fit is a
reparametrized `edges + nodematch("group")` and its coefficients match that model exactly
(`r round(coef(f_op), 3)[[1]]` and `r round(coef(f_op), 3)[[2]]`). the payoff comes when no
ready-made term exists — "gwesp among same-sex dyads only" is one `F()` away, not a feature
request. one more thing in that chunk: `control = snctrl(seed = 6886)` is the ergm-4
**cross-function control shorthand** — the same `snctrl()` call works as the `control =` for
`ergm()`, `simulate()`, `gof()`, `san()`, and friends, and dispatches to the right
`control.*()` constructor, so you can stop remembering which function wants
`control.gof.ergm()` versus `control.ergm()`.
:::

<span class="sub">back at 01:49 on the session clock — we broke early to buy the new last

the part you will actually use. nothing after the break depends on your having fit anything

# block C — failure, fit, value, and time [01:49 – 02:54]{.tm} {#block-c}

## C1 · degeneracy, live [01:49 – 02:07]{.tm} {#c1}

let us run the model i put on screen before the break. i am not going to hide what happens.

```{r}
#| label: c1-degenerate
#| error: true
m_tri <- ergm(mesa ~ edges + triangle,
              control = control.ergm(seed = 6886))
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

read that message, because it is one of the more useful error messages in R:

> *Number of edges in a simulated network exceeds that in the observed by a factor of more
> than 20. This is a strong indicator of model degeneracy or a very poor starting parameter
> configuration.*

here is what happened. remember step 3 of MCMC-MLE: simulate networks at the current $\theta$
and compare their statistics to the observed. `ergm` set out to do that, simulated from a model
with a triangle term, and the simulated networks came back with **more than twenty times** as
many edges as mesa has. it then stopped, on purpose, rather than burn twenty minutes walking
toward nothing.

### why triangles do this

the intuition is short and it is worth having. adding a tie that closes a triangle makes
further triangles easier to close, which makes further ties more attractive, which closes more
triangles. with a positive triangle coefficient the model has a **positive feedback loop** in
it, and the probability mass collapses onto the extremes of the sample space — the empty graph
and the complete graph — with almost nothing in between. real networks live in between.
so the model puts essentially no probability on anything that looks like your data.

formally this is *instability* in the sense of Schweinberger (2011): statistics that can grow
faster than linearly in the number of dyads make the log-likelihood dominated by extremal
graphs. the term "degeneracy" gets used loosely; that is the precise version.

::: {.callout-important title="statnet's own framing, and it is the right one"}
> "**unwanted degeneracy is an indicator of a poorly specified model. it is not a property of
> all ERGMs** (nor is it unique to ERGMs!) ... if your system is not degenerate but your model
> is, this suggests that you may need to rethink the theoretical motivation behind your choice
> of model terms."
>
> — the current statnet ERGM workshop tutorial

this is statnet's position, and meaningfully softer than the 2011-era "ERGMs are fragile"
story. the standing counter-view (Schweinberger 2011; Chatterjee & Diaconis 2013) is that for
many natural parameterizations near-degeneracy is a structural feature, not merely user error —
which is precisely why geometrically-weighted terms, and later LOLOG (see the wrap), had to be
invented. **degeneracy is information about your specification.** the model just told
you that the process you wrote down could not have produced your data. that is a finding.
:::

### the repair: geometric weighting

the problem is that each additional shared partner is worth as much as the first. the fix is a
term where each additional shared partner is worth *less* than the last — a geometrically
weighted count. that is `gwesp`: geometrically weighted edgewise shared partners.

```{r}
#| label: c1-gwesp
m2 <- fit_or_load("m2_gwesp",
  ergm(mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Sex") +
         gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
```
[slow ~20s]{.rt .rt-slow}

```{r}
#| label: c1-gwesp-summary
summary(m2)
```

it converges. `gwesp` is `r round(coef(m2)[["gwesp.fixed.0.25"]], 2)`, strongly positive:
mesa has substantially more triadic closure than grade and sex homophily alone can explain.
that is a real, defensible finding about adolescent friendship, and it is exactly the
statement that the naive `triangle` term could not deliver.

notice also that grade homophily **dropped** from `r round(coef(m1)[["nodematch.Grade"]], 2)`
to `r round(coef(m2)[["nodematch.Grade"]], 2)`. resist the urge to narrate that as "homophily
was partly spurious closure" — that is precisely the across-specification comparison Duxbury
warns about in [B2](#b2). part of that drop is rescaling. you cannot tell how much from these
two numbers.

::: {.callout-important title="two hard rules, both of which will bite you"}
**1. write `fixed = TRUE` unless you specifically intend a curved model.** as of `ergm` 4.0,
if you write `gwesp(0.25)` without `fixed = TRUE`, the decay value you typed is **silently
ignored** and you get a curved model that estimates decay instead. it is not a subtle
difference:

```{r}
#| label: c1-fixed
#| warning: false
rbind(unfixed_0.25 = summary(samplike ~ gwesp(0.25))[1:5],
      unfixed_0.90 = summary(samplike ~ gwesp(0.90))[1:5])
c(fixed_0.25 = summary(samplike ~ gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE)),
  fixed_0.90 = summary(samplike ~ gwesp(0.90, fixed = TRUE)))
```

the two unfixed rows are **byte-identical** — the decay argument did nothing. the two fixed
values differ, as they should. `ergm` does warn, but the warning scrolls past in a wall of
MCMC output. i have found this bug in published replication code more than once.

**2. never load a cached `ergm` fit from an old version.** `summary.ergm` compares the stored
version against the *current* major.minor, so under `r as.character(packageVersion("ergm"))`
*any* object saved from any earlier version warns. there is no version to freeze on — this
recurs at every release. it is also the single best argument for the format of this document:
everything you are looking at was refit today.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — where does 0.25 come from, and the honest answer is: nowhere good"}
that decay value is a convention, and the convention is under real pressure.

Stewart, Schweinberger et al. (*Social Networks*) show that geometrically weighted terms are
nonlinear functions of the *product* of the base and decay parameters, so the two are "mixed
up, and difficult to estimate," and a single network "may not contain much information about
decay parameters (in the statistical sense of Fisher information)." their practical finding is
uncomfortable: **fixing decay at a value other than its MLE changes the estimates of all the
other parameters**, and can hurt both in-sample and out-of-sample performance. their own
estimated decay was **0.913**, nowhere near the conventional 0 or 0.25.

so: everybody fixes decay because estimating it from one network is unstable, and the best
current evidence says fixing it biases everything else. that is a live, unresolved tension and
i would rather you knew about it than repeated "0.25 because that is what people use." their
proposed remedy is *multiple* networks, which supply the missing information — see
`ergm.multi`, and the ancillary document on that if you have data shaped that way.
:::

```{r}
#| label: c1-checkpoint
checkpoint(gwesp = coef(m2)[["gwesp.fixed.0.25"]],
           grade = coef(m2)[["nodematch.Grade"]],
           label = "CHECKPOINT C1")
```

## C2 · diagnostics: separation first, then mixing, then fit [02:07 – 02:20]{.tm} {#c2}

three checks, in the order you should actually run them — then the one tool underneath all
three. the order matters and almost nobody teaches it this way.

### 1. look at your cells *before* you fit

we have not touched `Race` yet. the natural specification is `nodematch("Race", diff = TRUE)`,
which gives a separate homophily parameter per racial category. before running it, look at the
mixing matrix:

```{r}
#| label: c2-mixing
mixingmatrix(mesa, "Race")
```

**look at the diagonal.** `Black`–`Black` is `r mixingmatrix(mesa,"Race")["Black","Black"]`
and `Other`–`Other` is `r mixingmatrix(mesa,"Race")["Other","Other"]` —
`r sum(mesa %v% "Race" == "Black")` black students,
`r sum(mesa %v% "Race" == "Other")` "other" students, and *none* of them friends with each other. that is perfect separation:
ask for a homophily parameter on a category where homophily never occurs and the maximum
likelihood answer is negative infinity. watch:

```{r}
#| label: c2-inf
m_race <- ergm(mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Race", diff = TRUE),
               control = control.ergm(seed = 6886))
data.frame(estimate = round(coef(m_race), 3))
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

two `-Inf` coefficients, exactly the two empty diagonal cells. this is not a numerical
failure — it is the right answer to the question you asked. the fix is to ask a better
question: restrict the term to levels that can actually be estimated.

```{r}
#| label: c2-levels
m_race2 <- ergm(
  mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Race", diff = TRUE,
                           levels = c("White", "Hisp", "NatAm")),
  control = control.ergm(seed = 6886))
data.frame(estimate = round(coef(m_race2), 3))
```

finite, interpretable, and you know exactly which groups you did and did not learn about.
**thirty seconds with `mixingmatrix()` before fitting saves you an afternoon of wondering why
your model returned infinity.** this generalises well beyond `nodematch` — any categorical
term with sparse cells has this problem.

### 2. did the chain actually mix?

for any dyad-dependent model, the coefficients are only as good as the MCMC that produced
them. `mcmc.diagnostics()` shows you the sampled network statistics, centred on their observed
values.

```{r}
#| label: c2-mcmc
#| fig-height: 5.5
mcmc.diagnostics(m2, vars.per.page = 4)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

what you want: trace plots that look like fuzzy horizontal caterpillars centred near zero, and
roughly symmetric densities. what you do not want: trends, long excursions, or a chain that
wanders off and stays there. these look fine.

if they had not, the moves are, in order: more iterations (`MCMC.burnin`, `MCMC.interval`),
then a different specification. in practice it is nearly always the specification.

### 3. goodness of fit — two different questions

`gof()` answers "if the model is true, does it generate networks that look like mine?" but
there are two versions of that question and people routinely run only the second one.

**in-model first.** did the model reproduce the statistics it was explicitly fitted on? this
is `GOF = ~model`, it is fast, and it returns a **table**, which for the 26 of you on laptops
is worth a great deal more than a plot:

```{r}
#| label: c2-gofmodel
set.seed(6886)
gof(m2, GOF = ~model)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

each row: the observed value, the range across simulated networks, and a monte carlo p-value.
high monte-carlo p-values mean the observed statistic sits comfortably inside the simulated
distribution. good — though note this is close to a minimum requirement rather than
an achievement. a model that cannot reproduce its own sufficient statistics has not converged.

**out-of-model second, and this is the real test.** simulate from the fit and compare features
you did *not* fit on. if the model captures the generative process, it should get those right
too, for free.

```{r}
#| label: c2-gof
#| fig-height: 6.5
g2 <- gof(m2)
plot(g2)
```
[live ~3s]{.rt .rt-live}

the default suite for an undirected network is degree distribution, edgewise shared partners,
and geodesic distance. black line observed, boxplots simulated: where the line sits inside
the boxes, the model reproduces a feature it was never fitted to.

::: {.callout-note title="this is the same move you already know"}
this is exactly the posterior predictive logic from the social relations model day: simulate
from the fitted model, compare to the observed data, and look for systematic discrepancy.
different implementation, identical epistemics. that is the third time this course has come
back to it, and it is not an accident — simulation-based adequacy checking is close to the
only general-purpose model criticism that works for network data.
:::

### 4. and the tool underneath all of it: `simulate()`

`gof()` is a convenience wrapper around something you can, and should, do with your own hands:
**draw networks from the fitted model**. the day opened with null models in [A1](#a1); a
fitted ERGM *is* a null model, tuned to your data, and `simulate()` is how you draw from it.

```{r}
#| label: c2-simulate
sims <- simulate(m2, nsim = 100, seed = 6886,
                 output = "stats", monitor = ~ triangle)
summary(mesa ~ triangle)
round(quantile(sims[, "triangle"], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)), 1)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

read the two arguments that do the work. `output = "stats"` says: do not keep the hundred
networks, keep their statistics. `monitor = ~ triangle` says: also track a statistic that is
**not in the model** — `m2` has `gwesp`, not `triangle`. so this is the out-of-model gof
logic, hand-built in two lines: mesa has `r summary(mesa ~ triangle)[[1]]` triangles, and the
model we fitted — which was never told to match triangles — puts its median draw at
`r round(quantile(sims[, "triangle"], 0.5))`, with the observed count sitting comfortably
inside the middle 95% of `r round(quantile(sims[, "triangle"], 0.025), 1)` to
`r round(quantile(sims[, "triangle"], 0.975), 1)`. that is `gwesp` earning its keep on a
statistic it was not fitted to.

now connect this
backwards: this is *exactly* the machine inside step 2 of MCMC-MLE from [A2](#a2), and it is
the machine the degeneracy guard in [C1](#c1) was running when it simulated from
`edges + triangle`, saw twenty times too many edges, and pulled the plug. one function,
underneath the entire day.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — what GOF cannot do, and why AIC is on thin ice here"}
`gof()` has two real limits.

**it is a check, not a comparison.** it tells you whether *this* model reproduces *those*
statistics. it gives you no way to rank two competing models, and there is a mild circularity
in that you choose the statistics to check.

**and the usual model-selection tools are shakier than they look.** `ergm` will happily print
AIC and BIC. Yin, Phillips & Butts (arXiv:1908.05873) make the sharp version of the objection:
those criteria "assume conditional independence of observations and/or conventional asymptotics,
and their theoretical foundations are not always applicable in a network modeling context." you
have one network. there is no growing sample of independent observations. their proposal is the
HOPE scheme — held-out predictive evaluation, cross-validation for networks.

worth knowing: `ergm` computes the log-likelihood by bridge sampling and now reports a
**standard error** on it, which is an underappreciated bit of honesty. if you are comparing
AICs that differ by less than that, you are comparing noise.

there is also a deeper problem in the background, Shalizi & Rinaldo (2013, *Annals of
Statistics*): most network data are *sampled subnetworks*, and inference implicitly assumes
the model is consistent under sampling (projective). triangle-like terms violate this, so "given
an ERGM for a large network, it cannot be the case that the induced model for any sub-network
must be the same" — standard asymptotics do not hold. practically: an ERGM fitted to a sampled
network does not straightforwardly estimate parameters of the population network. this is not
a reason to avoid ERGMs; it is a reason to be careful about what your network *is*.
:::

### tiered exercise (take-home — we will not fit this live)

> in the room i will read the prompt and show the solution tab; the actual fitting is for you
> to do afterwards, when nobody is waiting on a 40-second `gwesp` fit. the solution is complete
> and seeded, so your numbers will match mine exactly.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## core

add `nodefactor("Grade")` to `m2` and refit. in one sentence, say what it tests that
`nodematch("Grade")` does not.

```{r}
#| label: c2-ex-core
#| eval: false
m3 <- ergm(mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Sex") +
             gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) + ______,
           control = control.ergm(seed = 6886))
```

## stretch

`Race` has near-empty cells, as we saw. diagnose with `mixingmatrix()` **before** fitting, then
fit a model with `nodematch("Race", diff = TRUE)` restricted to estimable levels *plus*
`gwesp`. report the AME for the largest race-homophily effect, and state the baseline density
alongside it. then say why you would be cautious about the `NatAm` estimate specifically.

## solution

```{r}
#| label: c2-ex-soln
m3 <- fit_or_load("m3_nodefactor",
  ergm(mesa ~ edges + nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Sex") +
         gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) + nodefactor("Grade"),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
data.frame(estimate = round(coef(m3), 3))
```
[slow ~20s]{.rt .rt-slow}

**core.** `nodematch("Grade")` tests **homophily** — whether ties form *between* students of
the same grade. `nodefactor("Grade")` tests **activity** — whether students in a given grade
form more ties *overall*, regardless of who the partner is. one is about sorting, the other is
about volume, and they are completely different claims.

here the `nodefactor` coefficients are all **positive** relative to the reference category
(grade 7) and rise more or less monotonically, from
`r round(coef(m3)[["nodefactor.Grade.8"]],2)` for grade 8 up to
`r round(coef(m3)[["nodefactor.Grade.12"]],2)` for grade 12. so older students in this school
are *more* active, not just differently sorted — and note that grade homophily is still
strongly positive (`r round(coef(m3)[["nodematch.Grade"]],2)`) once activity is controlled
for. sorting and volume are both real and they are not the same thing.

**stretch.**

```{r}
#| label: c2-ex-soln2
m4 <- fit_or_load("m4_race",
  ergm(mesa ~ edges +
         nodematch("Race", diff = TRUE,
                   levels = c("White", "Hisp", "NatAm")) +
         gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
data.frame(estimate = round(coef(m4), 3))
ame(m4, "nodematch.Race.White")
c(baseline_density = network.density(mesa))
```
[live ~12s]{.rt .rt-live}

white–white homophily is the largest of the three (`r round(coef(m4)[["nodematch.Race.White"]],2)`,
against `r round(coef(m4)[["nodematch.Race.Hisp"]],2)` for hispanic and
`r round(coef(m4)[["nodematch.Race.NatAm"]],2)` for native american). its AME is
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100*ame(m4,"nodematch.Race.White")[["AME"]])` percentage points, against a
baseline density of `r round(network.density(mesa), 4)` — so it shifts the tie probability by
roughly `r sprintf("%.1f", ame(m4,"nodematch.Race.White")[["AME"]]/network.density(mesa))`× the
baseline while remaining well under one percentage point in absolute terms. report both,
exactly as in [B2](#b2).

**why be cautious about `NatAm`:** the mixing matrix shows
`r mixingmatrix(mesa,"Race")["NatAm","NatAm"]` within-`NatAm` ties out of a group
of `r sum(mesa %v% "Race" == "NatAm")` students, which is plenty of data — that one is fine.
the genuinely fragile estimate is
`White`, with only `r mixingmatrix(mesa,"Race")["White","White"]` within-group ties among
`r sum(mesa %v% "Race" == "White")` students. a category can be large enough to avoid `-Inf` and still be small enough that the
estimate is driven by a handful of dyads. "not infinite" is not the same as "well identified."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="the full toolbox — model assessment beyond the core path · self-study, not on the clock"}
three tools the timed path walks past. each closes a loop something above opened.

**`anova()` — nested model comparison, done properly.**

```{r}
#| label: tb-assess-anova
anova(m0, m1)
```

an analysis-of-deviance table across nested fits. it is fully valid here because `m0` and `m1`
are dyad-independent, so the likelihoods are exact. for MCMC fits the log-likelihood is
bridge-sampled and carries its own standard error — the AIC caution in the depth box above
applies to this table too, so do not lean on small deviance differences between dependent
models. one place this genuinely earns its keep: the `nodematch` help page itself recommends
an `anova()` of uniform (`diff = FALSE`) against differential (`diff = TRUE`) homophily.

**`predict()` — the packaged version of B2's hand arithmetic.**

```{r}
#| label: tb-assess-predict
head(predict(m1), 3)
```

one row per dyad; `p` is $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\theta^\top \delta)$ — the very numbers our
three-line `ame()` built from `ergmMPLE()` in [B2](#b2), now with a stable API around them.
the default `conditional = TRUE` evaluates at the observed graph, exactly as our version did;
`conditional = FALSE` simulates from the model instead, which is the equilibrium-distribution
answer to the first caveat in B2's depth box.

**`simulate()` for one whole network — seeing is believing.** the timed path drew simulated
*statistics* from `m2`; you can also ask for the graph itself and put it next to the data:

```{r}
#| label: c2-simulate-net
#| fig-height: 4
one <- simulate(m2, nsim = 1, seed = 6886, output = "network")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
set.seed(6886)
plot(mesa, vertex.col = "Grade", vertex.cex = 0.7, main = "observed")
plot(one,  vertex.col = "Grade", vertex.cex = 0.7, main = "one draw from m2")
```

the draw has `r network.edgecount(one)` edges to mesa's `r network.edgecount(mesa)` — same
sparse, grade-sorted, locally clumpy world, different in every particular.

**`gof()` with a suite you chose.** the default panel is a *choice*, not a law:

```{r}
#| label: tb-assess-gof
#| fig-height: 6.5
g_suite <- fit_or_load("tb_gof_suite",
  gof(m2, GOF = ~ degree + esp + distance,
      control = control.gof.ergm(nsim = 200, seed = 6886)))
plot(g_suite)
```

`GOF =` names the statistics; `control.gof.ergm(nsim =)` sets the number of simulated
networks (the default is 100 — doubling it steadies the boxplot whiskers). the rule worth
keeping: **if a statistic matters to your substantive argument, put it in the suite and report
it** — do not let the default panel decide what "fits well" means for your paper.
:::

```{r}
#| label: offroad-2
#| eval: false
# ---- live space: questions from the room go here ----
```

```{r}
#| label: c2-checkpoint
set.seed(6886)
gm <- gof(m2, GOF = ~model)
checkpoint(gof_model_p = round(gm$pval.model[, "MC p-value"], 2),
           label = "CHECKPOINT C2")
```

## C3 · valued ERGMs — when a tie is not 0/1 [02:20 – 02:36]{.tm} {#c3}

everything so far has assumed ties are binary. often they are not: trade volumes, message
counts, how many times one person nominated another. this is the Krivitsky (2012) reading, and
we can discharge it honestly in about fifteen minutes without leaving the monastery.

sampson observed his monks at **three** time points. `ergm` ships all three waves, so we can
build a count — how many of the three waves did $i$ nominate $j$?

```{r}
#| label: c3-data
suppressMessages(library(ergm.count))
data(samplk)
tot <- as.matrix(samplk1) + as.matrix(samplk2) +
       as.matrix(samplk3)
table(tot)
```

so most pairs never nominate each other; 30 pairs did so in all three waves. that is a valued
network with values 0–3.

```{r}
#| label: c3-net
nw <- as.network(tot, directed = TRUE, matrix.type = "adjacency",
                 ignore.eval = FALSE, names.eval = "nom")
nw
```

### the idea you have to get: sufficient statistics are not enough

with binary ties, writing down $g(y)$ fully specifies the model. **with valued ties it does
not.** if a tie can be any non-negative integer, you have to say something about the shape of
the distribution *before* the statistics do their work — is a value of 5 twice as surprising as
a 2? is there an upper bound?

that "something" is the **reference measure**. it fixes the sample space and the baseline
distribution against which $\theta^\top g(y)$ tilts. `ergm.count` implements Poisson, binomial,
geometric and discrete-uniform. Poisson is the sane default for counts.

`sum` is the valued analogue of `edges`: the sum of all tie values, so its coefficient controls
overall volume.

```{r}
#| label: c3-v1
v1 <- fit_or_load("v1_sum",
  ergm(nw ~ sum, response = "nom", reference = ~Poisson,
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
round(summary(v1)$coefficients, 4)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

`sum` is **`r round(coef(v1)[["sum"]], 3)`** — negative. read naively: monks nominate each
other less than a Poisson baseline would predict.

that reading is wrong, and here is how you find out.

```{r}
#| label: c3-v2
v2 <- fit_or_load("v2_sumnonzero",
  ergm(nw ~ sum + nonzero, response = "nom", reference = ~Poisson,
       control = control.ergm(seed = 6886)))
round(summary(v2)$coefficients, 4)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

**`sum` has changed sign: `r round(coef(v1)[["sum"]], 3)` → `r round(coef(v2)[["sum"]], 3)`.**

this is the whole Krivitsky lesson in two models. a bare Poisson reference cannot accommodate
how many **zeros** a real network has — `r sum(tot == 0) - nrow(tot)` of the
`r nrow(tot) * (nrow(tot) - 1)` ordered pairs here never nominate at all (the `table()` above
prints `r sum(tot == 0)` zeros, but `r nrow(tot)` of those are the structural diagonal — a monk
cannot nominate himself). with no way to represent that, the only lever the model has is to push overall volume down, so
`sum` goes negative. it is not measuring low volume; it is absorbing excess zeros.

add `nonzero` — a term that separately controls how many ties exist at all — and the two jobs
separate. `nonzero` is `r round(coef(v2)[["nonzero"]], 2)`, strongly negative, capturing the
sparsity. and now `sum` tells you the truth: **conditional on a nomination existing at all,
monks nominate each other *more* than Poisson predicts.**

the general lesson transfers directly: **in valued models, zero-inflation will masquerade as a
volume effect unless you give the model a way to represent zeros separately.** if you fit a
valued ERGM with only `sum`, you have almost certainly mis-read your own coefficient.

::: {.callout-warning title="the caveat ergm prints, which you should read"}
every valued fit prints this, and it is easy to scroll past:

> *Null model likelihood calculation is not implemented for valued ERGMs at this time. This
> means that all likelihood-based inference (LRT, Analysis of Deviance, AIC, BIC, etc.) is only
> valid between models with the same reference distribution and constraints.*

so you may compare our two models by AIC — same reference, same constraints. you may **not**
compare a Poisson-reference model to a geometric-reference model that way. that comparison
appears in the literature and it is not valid.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — what else is in there, and where to go next"}
`ergm.count` has a full vocabulary beyond `sum` and `nonzero`: `nodesqrtcovar`, `nodecovar`,
`transitiveweights()` with choices of two-path, combining and affecting functions, and so on.
`transitiveweights` in particular is the valued analogue of triadic closure, and — as in the
binary case — the choice among its variants matters and is under-discussed.

i am deliberately not doing that taxonomy today. fifteen minutes buys you the reference-measure
concept and the zero-inflation trap, which is what you need to read a valued ERGM paper without
being fooled. the taxonomy needs an hour it does not have here, and it is in the ancillary
document `valued_ergm_depth.qmd`.

one practical note: `gof()` gained support for valued ERGMs in `ergm` 4.11, so the diagnostics
from [C2](#c2) apply here too. that is recent — papers from before about 2023 mostly could not
do it, which is why so few valued ERGM papers report goodness of fit.
:::

```{r}
#| label: c3-checkpoint
checkpoint(sum_alone = coef(v1)[["sum"]],
           sum_with_nonzero = coef(v2)[["sum"]],
           nonzero = coef(v2)[["nonzero"]],
           label = "CHECKPOINT C3")
```

## C4 · temporal ERGMs — when you have more than one snapshot [02:36 – 02:54]{.tm} {#c4}

cranmer & desmarais (2011), on today's reading list, name the ERGM's two chief limitations:
ties are binary, and the model sees a single cross-section. [C3](#c3) just closed the first
with krivitsky's reference measures. we close the second one right now, and the price is
smaller than you think — because a temporal ERGM is not a new model.

today's arc, said out loud: binary cross-sectional ([A](#block-a)–[C2](#c2)) → valued
([C3](#c3)) → temporal. three extensions of one exponential family.

suppose you observe the same network at several waves — $Y^1, Y^2, \ldots, Y^T$: friendships
each term, alliances each decade. make one assumption: **given last wave, this wave is
independent of everything earlier.** then the joint distribution factors into transitions,
and each transition gets [A2](#a2)'s equation:

$$\Pr(Y^2, \ldots, Y^T \mid Y^1) = \prod_{t=2}^{T} \Pr(Y^t \mid Y^{t-1}), \qquad
\Pr(Y^t \mid Y^{t-1}, \theta) = \frac{\exp\{\theta^{\top} g(Y^t,\, Y^{t-1})\}}{\kappa(\theta, Y^{t-1})}$$

look at the right-hand piece: it is the ERGM from [A2](#a2) with exactly one change — the
sufficient statistics $g(\cdot)$ may now reference the **previous** wave as well as the
current one. that is the entire extension (robins & pattison 2001; hanneke, fu & xing 2010).
this is the **TERGM**, and it is not a frontier — it is a 2001 idea with mature software.

::: {.callout-important title="the difference between an ERGM and a TERGM, stated once, precisely"}
a **cross-sectional ERGM conditions on nothing**: it models one snapshot, and its sufficient
statistics are configuration counts of that single graph. a **TERGM conditions each wave on
the last, and pools the transitions**: its statistics may reference $Y^{t-1}$, so every
coefficient now reads as a **wave-to-wave transition effect** — given where the network stood
last wave, what raises the conditional log-odds of this tie now — not a fact about one
photograph. and the assumption doing the work has changed with it: instead of "my snapshot is
one draw from the model," you are assuming **independence across waves given the past** —
once the model knows $Y^{t-1}$, earlier history adds nothing. that Markov assumption is the
new thing you owe your reader a defence of. everything else — change statistics, degeneracy,
`fixed = TRUE`, gof — carries over verbatim, because each conditional piece *is* an ERGM.
:::

two temporal statistics carry most of the value, both in `btergm`:

* `memory(type = "stability")` — last wave's dyad states as a dyadic covariate. ties are
  sticky, and this term's job is to soak up the stickiness so it stops masquerading as
  something more interesting.
* `delrecip()` — **delayed reciprocity**: if $j \to i$ existed last wave, is $i \to j$ more
  likely this wave? that is a question about *sequence*, which no cross-section can ask.
  (the same trick generalizes: an `edgecov` of last wave's two-paths gives you lagged triadic
  closure — closing this wave the two-paths that existed last wave.)

estimation, honestly, in one breath: **`btergm`** maximizes a pseudolikelihood (MPLE) —
fast, scales to many waves and big networks, intervals by bootstrap resampling, no true likelihood;
**`tergm`** (statnet) does MCMC-based conditional MLE and can split each transition into
separate **formation and dissolution** equations (the STERGM) — the right tool when "what
creates ties" versus "what preserves them" is your actual question, at real computational
cost. today, `btergm`.

### the data: 50 adolescents, three waves

the teenage friends and lifestyle panel ships inside `RSiena`: 50 scottish adolescents,
friendship at three waves, alcohol and smoking measured at every wave. `btergm` wants a
**list of `network` objects**, one per wave, with each wave's covariates attached to the
matching network:

```{r}
#| label: c4-data
#| cache: false
suppressMessages({ library(RSiena); library(btergm) })  # loaded HERE, not in setup
tw    <- list(s501, s502, s503)                 # three 50x50 adjacency matrices
tnets <- lapply(tw, function(m) network(m, directed = TRUE))
for (i in seq_along(tnets)) {
  network::set.vertex.attribute(tnets[[i]], "drink", s50a[, i])
  network::set.vertex.attribute(tnets[[i]], "smoke", s50s[, i])
}
sapply(tnets, network.edgecount)
```
[live <1s]{.rt .rt-live}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="stuck? — two things in that chunk that are deliberate"}
**the load order.** `btergm` gets loaded *here*, not at the top of the day, and that is not
sloppiness: the moment its namespace loads it overrides `ergm`'s plot and print methods for
gof objects. run [C2](#c2)'s `gof()` output after loading `btergm` and the plots break with a
baffling error. if that happens to you, restart R and run the day in order. package conflicts
of exactly this kind are endemic in the statnet ecosystem — it is also why the `network::`
prefix in the loop is not decoration.

**the loop.** in base R a `for` loop cannot modify a list element in place — R copies on
assignment. `network` objects break that rule: they carry an external reference, so
`set.vertex.attribute()` modifies in place and the loop genuinely works.
:::

### fit it twice: without the past, then with it

first, pretend this section does not exist — pool the three waves with no temporal terms, the
model a cross-sectional habit would write:

```{r}
#| label: c4-cross
#| cache: false
set.seed(6886)
t_cross <- fit_or_load("tergm_s50_cross",
  btergm(tnets ~ edges + mutual + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
                 nodecov("drink") + absdiff("drink") + nodematch("smoke"),
         R = 200, verbose = FALSE))
round(coef(t_cross), 3)
```
[live ~3s]{.rt .rt-live}

(note `fixed = TRUE` — [C1](#c1)'s trap follows you here, because `btergm` calls `ergm`'s
term machinery.) now hand the model last wave:

```{r}
#| label: c4-stab
#| cache: false
set.seed(6886)
t_stab <- fit_or_load("tergm_s50_stab",
  btergm(tnets ~ edges + mutual + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
                 nodecov("drink") + absdiff("drink") + nodematch("smoke") +
                 memory(type = "stability"),
         R = 200, verbose = FALSE))
round(coef(t_stab), 3)
```
[live ~1s]{.rt .rt-live}

watch what one temporal term does to the structural story. `mutual` falls from
`r round(coef(t_cross)[["mutual"]], 2)` to `r round(coef(t_stab)[["mutual"]], 2)`, and `gwesp`
from `r round(coef(t_cross)[["gwesp.OTP.fixed.0.25"]], 2)` to
`r round(coef(t_stab)[["gwesp.OTP.fixed.0.25"]], 2)`, the moment the model learns what the
network looked like last wave — while `memory` itself comes in at
`r round(coef(t_stab)[["edgecov.memory[[i]]"]], 2)` and is, as promised, doing enormous work.
that shrinkage is the whole argument for temporal modelling in one table: the pooled fit was
reporting "reciprocity" and "closure" that were partly just *persistence* — last term's
friendships still standing. the temporal term is not a decorative control. it is the
difference between estimating a process and estimating a photograph.

point estimates are not inference, so before anyone quotes these numbers: where are the
standard errors? there are none, **by design** — `btergm`'s uncertainty comes from the
bootstrap, and you ask for it with `confint()`:

```{r}
#| label: c4-confint
#| cache: false
round(confint(t_stab), 2)
```
[live <1s]{.rt .rt-live}

those are **percentile intervals from the `R = 200` pseudolikelihood bootstrap** we already
paid for at fit time — no SEs, no p-values, and that is not a bug; report the interval and
`R` in your paper, exactly as this table gives them. read it the usual way: `mutual`'s
interval of `r round(confint(t_stab)["mutual", "2.5%"], 2)` to
`r round(confint(t_stab)["mutual", "97.5%"], 2)` sits well clear of zero, while
`nodecov.drink` (`r round(confint(t_stab)["nodecov.drink", "2.5%"], 2)` to
`r round(confint(t_stab)["nodecov.drink", "97.5%"], 2)`) straddles it — drinkers are neither
more nor less active once everything else is in the model. (small quirk to expect:
`summary()` on a `btergm` object prints its table twice in the current release — cosmetic,
not two models.)

::: {.callout-warning title="yes, i just made the comparison [B2](#b2) forbade"}
that was a coefficient comparison across nested specifications — the duxbury trap. the narrow
defence: i am claiming *direction and rough size* of a shift too large to be pure rescaling,
not an effect size, and i am testing nothing. the defensible version is the AME comparison
from [B2](#b2), on the probability scale; the ancillary deep dive does it properly. the
packaged TERGM analogue of [B2](#b2)'s `ame()` is `btergm::interpret()` — conditional tie
probabilities from the fitted model (Leifeld, Cranmer & Desmarais 2018, *JSS*). we do not run
it today; `?interpret` has worked micro-, macro- and dyad-level examples.
:::

### tiered exercise (the last of the day — core in the room, stretch tonight)

::: {.panel-tabset}

## core

read the `memory` coefficient in `t_stab` off the output above. in one sentence: what does it
say about these friendships, and why is it *supposed* to be large?
(hint: what would the waves be, if it were zero?)

## stretch

add `delrecip()` to `t_stab` and refit (seed 6886, `R = 200`). what happens to `mutual`, and
what does `delrecip` measure that the cross-sectional `mutual` in [B3](#b3) cannot, even in
principle?

## solution

```{r}
#| label: c4-ex-soln
#| cache: false
set.seed(6886)
t_temp <- fit_or_load("tergm_s50_temp",
  btergm(tnets ~ edges + mutual + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
                 nodecov("drink") + absdiff("drink") + nodematch("smoke") +
                 memory(type = "stability") + delrecip(),
         R = 200, verbose = FALSE))
data.frame(term          = c("mutual", "gwesp", "memory", "delrecip"),
           stability_only = round(coef(t_stab)[c("mutual", "gwesp.OTP.fixed.0.25",
                                                 "edgecov.memory[[i]]", NA)], 3),
           plus_delrecip  = round(coef(t_temp)[c("mutual", "gwesp.OTP.fixed.0.25",
                                                 "edgecov.memory[[i]]",
                                                 "edgecov.delrecip[[i]]")], 3),
           row.names = NULL)
round(confint(t_temp)["edgecov.delrecip[[i]]", ], 3)
```
[live ~2s]{.rt .rt-live}

**core.** dyads overwhelmingly stay in whatever state they were in last wave — ties persist,
empty dyads stay empty. it is *supposed* to be big: its entire job is to absorb persistence so
that persistence stops leaking into reciprocity and closure. if it were zero, the waves would
be independent redraws of the network and the pooled fit `t_cross` would have been fine.

**stretch.** `mutual` barely moves again
(`r round(coef(t_stab)[["mutual"]], 2)` → `r round(coef(t_temp)[["mutual"]], 2)`) — the
persistence was already absorbed by `memory`. what `delrecip` adds is not a control but a new
claim: a tie extended to you last wave raises the log-odds of your returning it this wave by
`r round(coef(t_temp)[["edgecov.delrecip[[i]]"]], 2)`, with a bootstrap interval that excludes
zero. that is a statement about *which direction came first* — and no cross-sectional model of
any kind, ERGM or otherwise, can make it. cross-sectional `mutual` only knows that
reciprocated pairs are common; it cannot see the sequence.
:::

```{r}
#| label: c4-checkpoint
#| cache: false
checkpoint(mutual_pooled   = coef(t_cross)[["mutual"]],
           mutual_temporal = coef(t_stab)[["mutual"]],
           memory          = coef(t_stab)[["edgecov.memory[[i]]"]],
           label = "CHECKPOINT C4")
```

### one sentence for tomorrow, and the deep dive

the TERGM is **tie-oriented**: the unit that changes between waves is the dyad. tomorrow's
model — the stochastic actor-oriented model — is **actor-oriented**: the unit that changes is
an actor's choice. whether those two framings are rivals or complements is a genuine,
published dispute, and it is literally where day 5 opens. you now have a fitted TERGM of your
own; bring it to the argument.

everything past this — goodness of fit for TERGMs (including out-of-sample tie prediction),
the other `memory` types (`autoregression`, `loss`, `innovation` — "stability" is one of
four), `timecov()` for secular trends, formation versus dissolution, actors entering and
leaving the panel, a larger IR application, and the full dispute reading list — is in the
deep-dive companion `ancillary/tergm.qmd`, which starts exactly where this section stops.

# wrap — ERGMs and latent variable models, honestly [02:54 – 03:00]{.tm} {#wrap}

five minutes, and i want to be careful here, because it would be easy for me to be unfair.

on day 3 you fitted latent factor models — the AME framework, my own work. today you fitted
ERGMs. it would be convenient for me to tell you one beats the other. that is not true and the
literature does not say it.

**where they agree, which is most of the territory.** dyadic observations are not independent.
standard logit is misspecified for network data. omitted dependence biases the **coefficients**,
not merely the standard errors, and no robust/clustered SE repairs coefficient bias from a
misspecified mean. that is distinct from the design-based use case: when the mean is modeled
adequately and dependence is treated purely as a nuisance for inference, dyadic cluster-robust
SEs (the DCR approach, which gets a full session on day 6) are a legitimate, live tool — not settled to be
inconsistent. the stronger claim — that robust clustered SEs are *inconsistent* for grouped
discrete-choice data, and that complex network dependence prevents the node-wise partitioning
clustering requires — is Cranmer & Desmarais's (citing Greene), and it is contested by the
design-based camp (Aronow, Samii & Assenova; Graham). both literatures are allies against the same
enemy, and that enemy is the dyadic logit with robust standard errors that still dominates
several fields. both also assess models the same way: simulate from the fit, compare to the
observed data.

**where they genuinely differ — four axes, no winner.**

| | ERGM | latent factor / AME |
|---|---|---|
| what dependence *is* | a hypothesis to parameterize and test | a nuisance to absorb so $\beta$ is trustworthy |
| direction of specification | specify the **joint**; conditionals follow | specify a **conditional mean**; dyads independent *given* the latents |
| nature of the structure | deterministic function of the **observed** network | **unobserved random** quantities |
| how it fails | degeneracy; MCMC-MLE non-convergence; decay non-identification / projectivity | choosing $R$, label switching, MCMC mixing |

the subtle one, stated plainly: **AME does not abolish conditional independence. it conditions
on more.** dyads are still conditionally independent given $u_i^\top D v_j$.

**what neither can do from one cross-section.** separate triadic closure from homophily on an
*unobserved* attribute. that is Shalizi & Thomas (2010), which you met on day 3. an ERGM
parameterizes closure and tests it; AME absorbs it into the latent terms. neither identifies
the other, and no amount of cleverness with a single cross-sectional network will fix that.
**that is the actual state of the literature, and it is exactly the setup for day 5, tomorrow** — the
stochastic actor-oriented model's entire claim is that panel data breaks the tie.

**and then the thing i find genuinely interesting.** Box-Steffensmeier, Christenson & Morgan
(2018, *Political Analysis*) propose the frailty ERGM, which adds node-specific random
intercepts — "sociality effects" — drawn from a normal centred at zero, extended to separate
**sender and receiver effects** for directed networks, because unmeasured node attributes
otherwise cause "coefficient bias and model degeneracy."

that is the social relations model, inside an ERGM.

> here is the thing that should bother you. on day 2 you fit sender and receiver random effects
> and called it the SRM. the ERGM literature — a separate community — hit degeneracy, went
> looking for a fix, and landed on node-specific sender and receiver random intercepts. they
> rediscovered your day-2 model from the other side of the room.

the two traditions are converging on the same structure from opposite directions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="depth — the honest scorecard, and what i am not claiming"}
three things i want on the record, because they are easy to get wrong and colleagues will
catch you:

**i am not claiming "AME beats ERGM."** "Taking Dyads Seriously" mentions ERGMs in a single
footnote and estimates exactly zero of them. its comparison is against the dyadic GLM with
robust standard errors — which is what all three of its replication targets used. the paper's
opponent is the naive logit, not the ERGM.

**Cranmer & Desmarais are not attacking latent space models.** their sharp passage about
"applying standard regression" targets the practice of computing network statistics and
plugging them into a logit as covariates. the paragraph immediately after is explicitly
irenic: *"it is not our intention here to pit the ERGM against these alternative approaches...
the quest for a universally best method is quixotic."*

**and their own stated limits are worth noting**, because today quietly answered
them: they name ERGM's chief limitations as binary-only and cross-sectional-only. the first
was solved by Krivitsky, which you did in [C3](#c3). the second by temporal ERGMs, which you
fit yourself in [C4](#c4). the reading list has an internal arc, and today walked all of it.

for the strongest constructive critique from *inside* the ERGM camp, look at LOLOG (Fellows &
Handcock; Clark & Handcock 2022, *JRSS-A*), which models network growth under a latent node
ordering and claims to avoid degeneracy. useful fact: **LOLOG and ERGM are identical under dyadic
independence**, so everything in blocks A and B transfers directly, and the divergence is
exactly at the dependence terms. that this comes from Handcock, an ERGM founder, makes it
impossible to frame as camp warfare.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="the referee checklist — the actual takeaway for most of you"}
realistically most of this room will read more ERGMs than you fit. so here is the checklist
today built, and it is the deliverable:

1. **is dependence modelled or absorbed?** and does the paper say which?
2. **which structural terms, and why?** justified substantively, or reverse-engineered from fit?
3. **was `fixed = TRUE` used on the geometrically weighted terms?** if the decay was typed but
   not fixed, the reported model is not the model they think they fitted.
4. **is goodness of fit reported, and on which statistics?** in-model only is not enough.
5. **are coefficients compared across nested specifications?** if so, that comparison is
   invalid (Duxbury) — and it is extremely common.
6. **are effects reported on a scale a reader can use**, with the baseline density alongside?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="what we deliberately did not show — five tools, five pointers"}
today demonstrated everything you need to build, fit, diagnose, interpret and extend an ERGM.
five pieces of the machinery were left out on purpose, so that you know they exist and where
to look rather than wondering whether i forgot them:

* **`san()`** — simulated annealing: construct a network whose statistics hit target values.
  used internally for MCMC starting points; useful to you for building synthetic test
  networks. `?san`.
* **`ergm.godfather()`** — apply a scripted sequence of tie toggles to a network and watch
  the statistics change: the hand-crank version of the change-statistic machinery from
  [A3](#a3). `?ergm.godfather`.
* **`ergm.exact()` / `ergm.allstats()`** — the *exact* likelihood by brute-force enumeration
  of all $2^{\binom{n}{2}}$ graphs. only feasible for networks of roughly eight nodes or
  fewer, which is exactly what makes it the right tool for checking your intuitions about
  [A2](#a2)'s normalizing constant. `?ergm.exact`.
* **`offset()` / `Offset()`** — fix a coefficient at a *known* value instead of estimating it:
  the device behind size-adjusted parameterizations (Krivitsky, Handcock & Morris 2011) and
  hard structural zeros. `?ergmTerm` under "Offset"; the operator version is in the
  appendix-A list.
* **`obs.constraints =` and missing data** — `ergm()` treats `NA` edges as *unobserved rather
  than absent*, and can additionally model the observation process itself. if your network
  has genuinely missing dyads, this is the principled route — not imputing zeros.
  `?ergmConstraint`, and the observational-process section of Krivitsky, Hunter, Morris &
  Klumb (2023, *JSS*).

the other two stated omissions of the day have homes already: the full valued-ERGM taxonomy
is in `ancillary/valued_ergm_depth.qmd` ([C3](#c3)), and everything temporal beyond
[C4](#c4)'s two terms is in `ancillary/tergm.qmd`.
:::

### where we go next — day 5

absorb it (day 3) → **test it (today, day 4)** → identify it with time (day 5, tomorrow).

everything until [C4](#c4) conditioned on one cross-section, and we hit a hard wall: you
cannot separate closure from homophily on unobservables. C4 made the first move that waves
allow — condition on last wave, tie-oriented. tomorrow (day 5, the SAOM day — homework 4 is
due then) uses the same kind of panel data in a continuous-time, actor-oriented model to try
to break that wall properly — and opens by asking whether the model you fit today is the
right way to use waves at all. we will be equally honest about what that does
and does not buy. after that, day 6 stops adjusting models altogether and asks the causal
question directly, and day 7 puts every model from this week head-to-head on one dataset.

# appendix A — depth track {#appendix-a}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="what changed in ergm 4, for anyone reading older tutorials"}
the assigned Hunter et al. (2008) JSS paper describes `ergm` 2. we are on
`r as.character(packageVersion("ergm"))`. the things that will actually trip you up:

* **curved terms ignore `decay` unless `fixed = TRUE`** (4.0). demonstrated in [C1](#c1). this
  is the one that silently changes results.
* **`levels2 =` default flipped** in `nodemix` and `mm` — now `-1`, excluding the first level
  combination. reference cells in older output differ.
* **`base =` and `keep =` are gone** → use `levels =` and `nodes =`.
* **`fit$coef` → `fit$coefficients`.** use `coef(fit)` and stop worrying.
* **`control.ergm(SAN.control =, loglik.control =)` → `SAN =`, `loglik =`.**
* **term operators are new in 4.0** — `B()`, `F()`ilter, `Offset()`, `Symmetrize()`, `Sum()`,
  `S()`ubgraph, `Log()`, `Exp()`, and dyad-independent interactions via `TERM1:TERM2`. a pre-4
  lecture teaches specification as a fixed vocabulary; `ergm` 4 makes it compositional. this is
  the largest genuinely new capability and it is barely taught anywhere — the [B3](#b3)
  toolbox runs one (`F()` rebuilding `nodematch` from parts) so you have a working template.
* **`snctrl()` is the one control shorthand to remember** — `control = snctrl(seed = 6886)`
  works across `ergm()`, `simulate()`, `gof()`, `san()` and friends, dispatching to the right
  `control.*()` constructor. demonstrated in the [B3](#b3) toolbox.
* **new defaults**: `MCMLE.termination = "confidence"`, adaptive `MCMC.samplesize`, the
  `.triadic` proposal hint on by default (models with closure mix much better than they used
  to), and `MCMLE.density.guard` — the tripwire that saved us twenty minutes in [C1](#c1) and
  which simply did not exist before.
* **4.11**: `gof()` supports valued ERGMs; `samplk1/2/3` gained edge weights, which is why
  [C3](#c3) works on data you already knew.

the current companion paper is **Krivitsky, Hunter, Morris & Klumb (2023), *JSS* 105(6)**,
"ergm 4: New Features." read that alongside the 2008 paper, not instead of it — the 2008 GOF
section is still the best exposition of the logic.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="scaling up: what to do above ~1,000 nodes"}
plain MCMC-MLE has a practical ceiling around one to a few thousand nodes. above that there are
three real routes:

* **MPLE with bootstrap or Godambe standard errors** — built into `ergm` since 4.5, see
  [B1](#b1). the pragmatic default.
* **`bigergm`** (CRAN) — hierarchical ERGM, successor to `hergm`/`lighthergm`. recovers blocks
  first, then estimates within- and between-block effects, permitting dependence only *within*
  blocks (local dependence in the Schweinberger–Handcock sense).
* **`ergm.multi`** (CRAN, installed here) — not one big network but *many* networks. this is
  also the practical route to estimating decay properly, per the tension in [C1](#c1).

i have not run `bigergm` for you, so treat that row as documentation rather than a
recommendation. i mention all three because there are people in this room with data far larger
than mesa, and leaving you to discover that `ergm()` will not just work is a disservice.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="a netify handoff, if your data does not start as a network object"}
most of you will not receive data as a `network` object — you will have an edgelist and a node
table. `netify` gets you from one to the other without hand-writing conversion code:

```{r}
#| label: appendix-netify
#| cache: false
suppressMessages(library(netify))
data(classroom_edges); data(classroom_nodes)
cls <- netify(classroom_edges, actor1 = "from", actor2 = "to",
              symmetric = TRUE)
cls <- add_node_vars(cls, classroom_nodes, actor = "student")
cls_net <- netify_to_statnet(cls)
summary(cls_net ~ edges + nodematch("gender") +
          nodematch("grade"))
```

`r network.size(cls_net)` students, `r network.edgecount(cls_net)` friendships. that is **too
small to fit a credible ERGM** — `r network.edgecount(cls_net)` edges will not
support a `gwesp` term — so i am not modelling it. it is here purely to show the bridge from a
`netify` object to something `ergm()` accepts. day 1's netify session covered the rest.
:::
